content: 1. Mavacamten and Ethinylestradiol/Progestin: Mavacamten reduces the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol and progestin by inducing hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 enzyme metabolism. This interaction may result in contraceptive failure or increased breakthrough bleeding. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. Since ethinylestradiol and progestin are CYP3A4 substrates, systemic exposure to these hormones may decrease significantly. Patients should be advised to use a contraceptive method unaffected by CYP450 enzyme induction, such as an intrauterine system, or add a non-hormonal contraceptive method (e.g., condoms) during coadministration and for four months after the last dose of mavacamten. 2. Ethinylestradiol and Metyrapone: Ethinylestradiol decreases the effects of metyrapone through an unspecified interaction mechanism. This may lead to a subtherapeutic response to metyrapone in patients receiving estrogen therapy, including oral contraceptives. It is advisable to discontinue estrogen therapy prior to and during metyrapone administration. 3. Omaveloxolone and Hormonal Contraceptives: Omaveloxolone decreases the levels or effects of etonogestrel and other hormonal contraceptives (e.g., pills, patches, rings, implants, and progestin-only pills) by weakly inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. If hormonal contraceptives are used, an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 4. Mifepristone and Ethinylestradiol: Mifepristone increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. 5. Mycophenolate and Ethinylestradiol: Mycophenolate decreases the effects of ethinylestradiol through an unknown mechanism. Patients should consider using an alternative or additional form of contraception. 6. Nelfinavir and Ethinylestradiol: Nelfinavir can cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, either increasing or decreasing them, by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. This may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. 7. Nevirapine and Ethinylestradiol: Nevirapine decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 8. Omaveloxolone and Ethinylestradiol: Omaveloxolone decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. 9. Oxcarbazepine and Ethinylestradiol: Oxcarbazepine decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 10. Pentobarbital and Ethinylestradiol: Pentobarbital decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 11. Phenobarbital and Ethinylestradiol: Phenobarbital decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 12. Phenytoin and Ethinylestradiol: Phenytoin decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 13. Primidone and Ethinylestradiol: Primidone decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. The use of a non-hormonal contraceptive method is recommended. 14. Quinidine and Ethinylestradiol: Quinidine increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. 15. Ranolazine and Ethinylestradiol: Ethinylestradiol increases the levels or effects of ranolazine by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Patients should avoid this combination or use alternative drugs. 16. Repotrectinib and Ethinylestradiol: Repotrectinib decreases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Patients should use an effective non-hormonal contraceptive method.
